title: The envelope opens
summary: Ten weeks of a sealed envelope end this morning. Read the final's motion out loud, then build both cases properly, because the sides are drawn on the day and you will not know which one is yours until you are standing up.
materials: the sealed envelope from week 1, still sealed
two sheets of paper and a pen
the two minute and one minute sand timers

steps.title: Both cases, because the side is drawn on the day
steps.body:
Today the envelope comes off the shelf. Whatever is on that card is the motion for the final in two weeks, and at the final a coin decides which side you are defending. Not your preference. A coin.

That rule is doing a job. A debater who only ever argues the side they already believe is not learning to argue, they are learning to feel strongly out loud. Building the case you do not like is where the real work is, and it is also the fastest way to find out what your own side is actually standing on.

So the skill of the week is building two cases at once, and the discipline is simple: whatever you write on the page you agree with, you must write its opposite on the other page before you are allowed to feel good about it. Three claims a side, and every claim carries an evidence slot, exactly as in week 5. A claim with an empty evidence slot is a feeling with a suit on.

Steelman rule, still standing and now doing heavy lifting. The version of the other side you argue against must be the version their best debater would recognise. If your opposition case is easy to knock down, you built a scarecrow, and at the final the coin might hand you that scarecrow to defend.

One warning about research, because this is a research week. Anything you write in an evidence slot needs to say where it came from, in your own handwriting, next to it. A number with no source is not evidence, it is decoration. If you ask an AI for help, it will hand you fluent sentences that sound exactly like facts, and some of them will not be, so anything it gives you is a lead to check rather than a line to quote. And if you cannot find real evidence for a claim, that is not a disaster. Cross the claim off. You have just saved yourself from being cross-examined on it.

The week's question, which is not the same as the motion: is winning an argument the same as being right? You are about to spend a fortnight learning to win an argument you might not agree with. Worth knowing what that does and does not prove.

steps.title: Open it, then split the page in two
steps.body:
Take the envelope off the shelf. Open it in front of a grown-up, with the camera running if you want the moment. Read the motion out loud, twice, slowly.

First, before any arguing, work out what the motion actually says. Underline the one word that is going to be fought over, because every motion has one. Then write, in your own words, what the world looks like if the motion is true, and what it looks like if the motion is false. If those two pictures look the same, you have not understood the motion yet.

Now two sheets. Head one FOR and one AGAINST, with the motion copied at the top of both, word for word off the card. Nobody gets to reword a motion to suit themselves.

Three claims on each sheet. One claim per line, in a sentence you could say out loud in one breath, with a blank evidence slot under it waiting to be filled. Do not write the arguments in the order they occur to you. Write the FOR sheet's first claim, then the AGAINST sheet's first claim, then back again, so neither sheet gets your fresh brain and the other one your tired one.

When both sheets have three claims, do the swap. Read one sheet out loud as if you meant it, all three claims, in your best voice. Then read the other one the same way. A grown-up listens to both and tells you which one sounded like you believed it. That answer is useful, and it tells you which sheet needs another half hour.
checklist: The envelope was opened in front of someone and the motion was read out loud twice
The word the debate will turn on is underlined, and I said what the world looks like on each side of the motion
Both sheets carry the motion copied word for word from the card
Each sheet has three claims, one line each, with an evidence slot under every one
Both sheets were read out loud as if I meant them, and I was told which one sounded convinced

steps.title: Evidence, honestly gathered
steps.body:
Now fill the slots. Twenty minutes, and the rule is that both sheets leave the table with at least two slots filled.

What counts as evidence, roughly in order of how hard it is to argue with: a number from somewhere you can name; something that actually happened, told accurately, including the boring parts; what somebody who would know says, with who they are attached; and last, an example from your own life, which is real evidence but weak on its own, because the other side has a life too.

What does not count: what everybody knows, what feels obvious, and a statistic you cannot say the source of. If you catch yourself writing the word obviously, stop and put a number there instead.

Three habits for the twenty minutes. Write the source beside every piece of evidence, in your own handwriting, tight enough that you could find it again. Look for the evidence against your favourite claim on purpose, before your opponent finds it for you, because being surprised at the final is much more expensive than being surprised now. And when a piece of evidence is genuinely good for the side you do not like, write it on that sheet anyway. It is going to exist whether or not you write it down, and the only question is whether you meet it here at the kitchen table or in front of a judge.

Finish with a two minute test. Cover the AGAINST sheet, look at the FOR sheet, and say its three claims and their evidence out loud without reading them word for word. Then do the same with the other sheet. Whichever one falls apart is the one you work on this week.
checklist: At least two evidence slots are filled on each of the two sheets
Every filled slot has a source written next to it in my own handwriting
I went looking for evidence against my own favourite claim and wrote down what I found
Anything an AI gave me was checked somewhere else before it went in a slot, or it was left out
I said each sheet out loud from memory and named the sheet that fell apart

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record two things in one take. First, one minute making the best case for the side of the motion you like least, standing, with your sheet down and not in your hand. Then, still rolling, answer the week's question in your own words with a reason attached: is winning an argument the same as being right, and can you name a time somebody won an argument with you and was wrong anyway?
